note: Literature review and two critiques of the experimental plan, written before the runs of section 7 (2026-11-10). Paths inside the texts refer to the scratch directory of that session.

entries.topic: 1 FER/UFR hypothesis
entries.citation: Kumar, Clune, Lehman, Stanley (2025, revised Oct 2026). Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis. arXiv 2505.11581
entries.finding: Position paper. A Picbreeder-evolved image network (skull; butterfly and apple in the appendix) and an SGD-trained network of the same layered architecture produce the same image, but each hidden unit's response map is orderly and symmetric in the evolved network and patchy in the SGD one (the layered evolved skull network has only 24 distinct unit maps; the SGD network shows no symmetry in any of its 12 hidden layers). Sweeping single weights changes the evolved image coherently (mouth width, a wink) and the SGD image incoherently; a PCA change of basis and sweeps along random weight directions do not rescue the SGD network. No numerical measure of fracture is defined. Evidence for LLMs is behavioural and anecdotal (GPT-3 counting depending on object type, GPT-4o replacing numbers but not words at given positions) plus cited work on bags of heuristics. The authors state that they propose no method. A companion paper (Lehman and Stanley 2026, arXiv 2611.11020, abstract only) reports that unified networks forget less under fine-tuning.
entries.relevance: H1 runs against this source: it argues that conventional SGD yields fractured representations, and the UFO paper (section 8) says unified representations should not be expected from conventional training. Grokking is left open as a possible late unification. The paper's test of quality is how the output changes under weight perturbation (coherent or chaotic), not whether activation perturbations are damped, so U2 measures a different property. U1's compressibility is the UFO paper's proxy and has not been validated against these visual criteria.

entries.topic: 2 Co-training a model with an auxiliary reconstructor
entries.citation: Lai, Heimersheim (2025). SAE regularization produces more interpretable models. LessWrong, 28 Jan 2025
entries.finding: A character-level GPT-2 (4 layers, width 64, Shakespeare) is trained together with SAEs placed before and after every block. The SAE reconstruction loss, divided by the activation norm so that the model cannot simply shrink its activations, and the sparsity loss are added to the task loss (target L0 about 10). Fresh SAEs are then trained on the regularised weights. Averaged over ten model pairs, the loss increase from substituting SAE reconstructions at L0 about 50 is lower on every layer (least reliably on layer 3), also when reconstructions are substituted at all layers at once ('compound' loss increase). The regularised model reaches a slightly lower task loss; the authors caution that the dataset is small and overfits. Results are shown as plots, no numbers in the text.
entries.relevance: The one direct precedent for an SAE that 'communicates' with its network, but through gradients during training, not at inference. It shows that a network can be pulled towards SAE-decodable geometry at toy scale without loss. It does not test damping of perturbations, the lowest layers or real-time use (H2). Its substitute-at-every-layer measure is the precedent for running U4 at several blocks at once.

entries.topic: 2 Low-dimensional activation regulariser and grokking
entries.citation: Kazanskii (2026). How to Tame Grokking: Representation Geometry as a Control Signal. arXiv 2607.11666
entries.finding: Tracks the participation ratio of the activation covariance (effective dimensionality) per hidden layer during grokking and adds a penalty on the variance outside the top d* principal components (GeomDR), switched on after an initial phase. Without the penalty, dimensionality collapses before generalisation in every run: in the MLP baseline on modular addition the deepest layer falls to half its initial value at about 15-25K steps and grokking follows at about 250-500K. With the penalty MLPs grok up to 52.5x faster (362.1K to 6.9K steps); transformers only about 2x (addition 66.4K to 33.0K, division 89.4K to 48.7K steps; five seeds, 30 % training split). Targets d* of 16-64 help; d* of 8 or less slows and destabilises learning; switching the penalty on very early or late is worse.
entries.relevance: The PCA half of U6 would repeat this. Expect compressibility to rise well before validation accuracy and most strongly in the deepest layer, so 'appears when the network generalises' has to be tested as a lead-lag question. A very small linear bottleneck is a poor yardstick (d* of 8 or less hurts), which favours the non-linear 2-dim autoencoder for comparison with the UFO paper. Supports the weak form of H1: compression arises without any regulariser.

entries.topic: 2 Co-trained low-capacity reconstructors (the UFO paper's nearest relatives)
entries.citation: Sanyal, Kanade, Torr, Dokania (2018/2020). Robustness via Deep Low-Rank Representations. arXiv 1804.07090; Bhalodia, Elhabian, Kavan, Whitaker (2019). CoopSubNet: Cooperating Subnetwork for Data-Driven Regularization of Deep Networks under Limited Training Budgets. arXiv 1906.05441
entries.finding: Sanyal et al. attach a 'virtual' branch, unused at prediction time, that learns a rank-limited identity map of the activations of one or two layers of a ResNet-18/50 on CIFAR; its reconstruction error is back-propagated into the network. Result: low-rank activations, a modest accuracy gain, clearly higher robustness to Gaussian and adversarial input noise without adversarial training, and a 5-dim embedding that loses only 6 % accuracy. Even without the regulariser the activations before the last fully connected layer have an effective rank of about 10; the 16,384-dim layer before the fourth block is not low-rank unless regularised. Bhalodia et al. attach a non-linear autoencoder with a bottleneck (16-512 units) to the feature layer, train it jointly after a burn-in phase, normalise the reconstruction error by the feature norm, and find that this soft constraint beats a hard bottleneck when data are scarce (reduced MNIST, landmark and nuclei regression). Both read via the ar5iv full text.
entries.relevance: The link the user assumes, compressible representations go with damping of noise, is documented here for input noise in image classifiers. The unregularised rank of about 10 at the last layer shows that low-dimensional structure arises on its own late in a network but not earlier, so U1 should expect strong depth dependence. Neither paper perturbs hidden states or studies language models.

entries.topic: 3 Activation plateaus
entries.citation: Heimersheim, Mendel (2024). [Interim research report] Activation plateaus & sensitive directions in GPT2. LessWrong / Alignment Forum, 5 Jul 2024; follow-up: Giglemiani, Petrova, Mangat, Janiak, Heimersheim (2024). Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2. arXiv 2409.15019
entries.finding: GPT-2 small, perturbation of the residual stream before block 1 at the last position of 10-token texts, read-out by KL of the logits or distance at the last layer. (1) Around a real activation the output barely changes for small perturbations and then rises sharply (a plateau); around a random point drawn with the same mean and covariance it rises at once. (2) Moving towards another real activation leaves the plateau earlier than moving in a covariance-matched random direction; isotropic random directions are far less effective still. A typical distance between two activations is about 50. The authors read the plateau as the error correction that theories of computation in superposition require; in Sept 2024 they withdrew confidence in result (2). Giglemiani et al.: activations synthesised from SAE latents match real ones in directional sensitivity only when sparsity and latent co-occurrence are matched, and still show weaker plateaus.
entries.relevance: Answers U2's question about size in advance: the documented behaviour is suppression of small deviations followed by breakthrough, so relative damping falls as f grows. H2's brake for perturbations that become 'too large' is the reverse of this. U2 should report the plateau length per direction class and include sizes well below f = 0.1. The plateau exists around real states only, so a state that is already perturbed or SAE-reconstructed (U4) starts from a point with a weaker plateau.

entries.topic: 3 Stable regions (Qwen family, emergence in training)
entries.citation: Janiak, Karwowski, Mangat, Giglemiani, Petrova, Heimersheim (2024). Characterizing stable regions in the residual stream of LLMs. arXiv 2409.17113
entries.finding: Interpolates the residual state after the first block (last position) between two prompts and measures the change of the final state. In Qwen2 (0.5B-7B) and OLMo (1B, 7B), dissimilar prompts give a flat start, a sharp jump and a flat end; similar prompts give a straight line. The jump sharpens with model size and over training (OLMo checkpoints); randomly initialised models give nearly straight lines. One region boundary is crossed while hundreds to thousands of MLP gates change sign. After block 7 of Qwen2-1.5B the curve is smoother but still jumps. The authors report the same in GPT, Pythia, Phi and Llama, not in Gemma.
entries.relevance: The plateau is shown in the Qwen family and is learned, not architectural; this is the LLM-scale counterpart of U6's question. For U2 it predicts little effect of 'regular' perturbations until a boundary is crossed, then a switch of the output to the other text's continuation, so KL should be reported together with whose prediction the output moves to. Only interpolation between real states at one position was tested.

entries.topic: 3 Sensitivity by direction type (random, real, SAE feature, SAE error)
entries.citation: Lee, Heimersheim (2024). Investigating Sensitive Directions in GPT-2: An Improved Baseline and Comparative Analysis of SAEs. arXiv 2410.12555; Lindsey (2024). How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Anthropic Circuits Updates, April 2024
entries.finding: Lee and Heimersheim: GPT-2 small, residual stream before block 6, all positions, 2M tokens, KL against perturbation length. Directions that contain minus the current state (difference to another real or covariance-matched random state) change the output more than 'mixtures' (difference of two other states); real and covariance-matched mixtures behave almost alike; isotropic random directions are the weakest. Against the mixture baseline, replacing a state by its SAE reconstruction is no longer unusually harmful at block 6 (this varies by layer). SAE decoder directions of features inactive in the context always beat isotropic random; against the mixture baseline it depends on the SAE, sparser SAEs (lower L0) having stronger directions; end-to-end SAEs are not stronger. Along the SAE-error direction KL shows a plateau, then a roughly linear rise. Lindsey (4-layer model): ablating a feature costs much more loss than a random perturbation of equal size and more than doubling it; shrinking the whole state towards zero has little effect, almost none in later layers.
entries.relevance: U2's five direction classes are this design. Consequences: the 'regular' class as planned contains minus h and will look strong for that reason alone, so add the difference of two other real states; isotropic noise is a weak baseline, so add covariance-matched noise; split every perturbation into the part along h, which the normalisation layers remove, and the rest. Expected ordering in Qwen3: isotropic and low-variance directions below SAE-error and mixtures, below decoder directions. This matches the project's result that a move only a probe sees does not move the output.

entries.topic: 3 Growth of the residual norm with depth
entries.citation: Heimersheim, Turner (2023). Residual stream norms grow exponentially over the forward pass. LessWrong / Alignment Forum, 7 May 2023
entries.finding: Across GPT-2 sizes and other open models the norm of the residual state at each position grows roughly exponentially with depth, about 4.5 % per block in GPT-2 XL (blocks 5-41); attention and MLP outputs and their output-weight norms grow at the same rate. The first position (BOS) and padding positions behave differently. Some models show phases of decreasing norm. Favoured explanation: behind a normalisation layer a block cannot easily cancel what is already in the stream, but it can drown it out by writing something larger.
entries.relevance: The relative deviation |h'-h|/|h| in U2 will fall with depth for this reason alone, without any block writing against the perturbation. The persistence p_m separates the two cases, and the authors' conjecture predicts p_m near 1 (overshadowing, not cancelling). Qwen3's own norm profile has to be measured first, and the first position and extreme-norm positions excluded.

entries.topic: 3 Jacobian gains of transformer blocks
entries.citation: Fernando, Guitchounts (2026). Dynamics of the Transformer Residual Stream: Coupling Spectral Geometry to Network Topology. arXiv 2605.14258; see also Islam, Villarreal, Nishino, Salman, Liu (2026). Numerical Instability and Chaos: Quantifying the Unpredictability of Large Language Models. arXiv 2604.13206
entries.finding: Fernando and Guitchounts compute exact per-block Jacobians on 1,000 WikiText-2 samples for Llama 3.1 8B, OLMo 3 7B (also at initialisation and mid-training) and Gemma 4 E4B. About 98 % of eigenvalues are complex pairs (rotation plus stretch). Early blocks are strongly anisotropic (condition number about 10^6 in Llama blocks 0-4) and rotation-like; middle blocks have 17-30 % expanding modes; late blocks are near-symmetric because the identity path dominates. The product of Jacobians from block 0 to the end has an effective rank of 6.7 in Llama (of 4,096 directions), 5.9 in Gemma and about 42 in OLMo, against about 326 for OLMo at initialisation: training installs a funnel that passes a handful of directions and suppresses the rest. Islam et al. (abstract and introduction only): perturbations at floating-point rounding scale either amplify or vanish in the early blocks of Llama-3.1-8B, with three regimes (constant, chaotic, signal-dominated).
entries.relevance: The infinitesimal version of U2 is answered for three LLMs: almost all directions are attenuated end to end, a few are amplified, and this is learned. That supports a weak form of H1 (training builds a low-dimensional funnel) without showing a dedicated mechanism. It also says the lowest blocks are where amplification and loss are strongest, which speaks against H2's idea that they tolerate indeterminism. U2 adds finite size and direction classes; a randomly initialised Qwen3 as control would separate architecture from training, as their step-0 model does.

entries.topic: Neurons as units (starting point of the request)
entries.citation: Arora, Wu, Steinhardt, Schwettmann (2026). Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis. arXiv 2601.22594
entries.finding: Llama 3.1 8B (Gemma-2 2B/9B in the appendix), subject-verb agreement benchmark of Marks et al. Circuits built from MLP neuron activations (before the output projection) are about 100x smaller than circuits built from MLP outputs. With integrated gradients, neurons stay somewhat less sparse than SAE features; with the attribution method RelP about 200 neurons reach near-perfect faithfulness and completeness, on a par with SAE features. A city-state-capital case study is reproduced with small neuron sets that can be steered.
entries.relevance: Independent support for the starting point (MLP neurons as usable units) and for the project's own finding that 300-1,000 chosen neurons move the output. For U3 it gives the expected scale (about 100 neurons for one effect) and a warning that the ranking depends on the attribution method; U3's c_n is a direct-write measure and needs the planned clamping as check. Contrast: Gurnee et al. 2024 (entry on entropy neurons) find only 1-5 % of GPT-2 neurons recur across training seeds.

entries.topic: 4 Self-repair: Hydra effect and erasure by late MLPs
entries.citation: McGrath, Rahtz, Kramar, Mikulik, Legg (2023). The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations. arXiv 2307.15771
entries.finding: Chinchilla-type 7B model (32 layers, RMSNorm, trained without dropout), factual-recall prompts. Removing one attention layer makes a later attention layer increase its contribution to the correct logit (Hydra effect); late MLP layers normally push the most likely token down ('erasure') and do so less after the ablation. The compensation is local (few downstream layers change), explains 92 % of the variance of downstream changes at layer 23, and is incomplete: the regression slope of compensation on the removed effect is below 1 for all layers past 13.
entries.relevance: Shows a learned negative feedback on the output logit that arises without dropout, in a model with the same normalisation as Qwen3. It is partial, late and tied to the predicted token; it is not a general damper of arbitrary residual directions. For U3 it suggests where to look (late MLPs) and that restoring contributions will be concentrated in few blocks.

entries.topic: 4 Self-repair: role of the final normalisation and anti-erasure neurons
entries.citation: Rushing, Nanda (2024). Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models. arXiv 2402.15390
entries.finding: Resample-ablating single attention heads on 1M tokens of the pre-training distribution (Pythia-160M/410M/1B, GPT-2 small/medium, Llama-7B): later components restore part of the lost direct effect on the correct logit, imperfectly and noisily, sometimes over-correcting. Two mechanisms: (1) the final normalisation rescales the remaining logits (for one head the scale ratio exceeds 1 on 90.7 % of high-effect tokens), accounting for roughly 30 % on average; (2) sparse sets of MLP neurons that normally erase the head's output do so less ('anti-erasure'); these neurons differ from prompt to prompt, and about 60 % of neurons do not change. The authors propose 'iterative inference' (each block reduces the remaining error of a running guess), under which self-repair is a by-product. McDougall et al. 2023 (arXiv 2310.04625, abstract only): copy suppression explains 39 % of self-repair in one narrow task.
entries.relevance: For U3: expect sparse, prompt-specific neuron sets, so a fixed top-N list chosen on one set of texts may not transfer; measure the share that runs through the final RMSNorm scale separately before crediting neurons. Self-repair is defined here on the correct-token logit after ablations; whether the same neurons act against generic perturbations is open and is what U3 would add.

entries.topic: 5 Entropy / confidence-regulation neurons
entries.citation: Gurnee, Horsley, Guo, Kheirkhah, Sun, Hathaway, Nanda, Bertsimas (2024). Universal Neurons in GPT2 Language Models. arXiv 2401.12181; Stolfo, Wu, Gurnee, Belinkov, Song, Sachan, Nanda (2024). Confidence Regulation Neurons in Language Models. arXiv 2406.16254; Du et al. (2025). How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs. arXiv 2504.02904
entries.finding: Gurnee et al. found them through weight statistics: a last-layer neuron of GPT-2 medium with the 15th-largest weight norm and the smallest variance of its direct effect on the logits. Fixing it high raises the final normalisation scale, squeezes all logits like a higher temperature and raises entropy without reordering tokens; a second neuron writing the opposite direction (cosine -0.886) lowers entropy. Stolfo et al.: these neurons write into directions the unembedding almost ignores (in GPT-2 small the singular values drop to near zero from about index 755 of 768) and act through the final normalisation. That path carries about 80 % of their effect in GPT-2, Phi-2 and LLaMA2-7B (RMSNorm) and 30-40 % in Pythia and Gemma 2B; a model trained with dropout has a larger such subspace; on repeated text one neuron raises entropy as a hedge (clipping it lowers entropy by up to 70 %, 20 % on natural text). Du et al.: the ten such neurons of Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B largely coincide between base and instruct versions. No study on a Qwen model was found.
entries.relevance: U5's search and clamp test would replicate this in a new model family; the recipe (top weight norm, lowest logit variance or share of write norm in the bottom singular directions of the unembedding) is ready. Confound: any noise adds norm in the ignored directions and so raises entropy through the final RMSNorm with no regulation involved, so the late-noise control must match the norm added in that subspace. Qwen3-1.7B ties input and output embeddings (config checked), as GPT-2 does.

entries.topic: 6 Replacing activations by SAE reconstructions
entries.citation: Gurnee (2024). SAE reconstruction errors are (empirically) pathological. LessWrong / Alignment Forum, 29 Mar 2024; Engels, Smith, Tegmark (2024/2025). Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders. arXiv 2410.14670
entries.finding: Gurnee: GPT-2 small, residual-stream SAEs (32x), 2M tokens, substitution at all positions of one layer. Replacing the state by its SAE reconstruction raises KL and loss 2.2-4.5x more than replacing it by a random point at the same distance, at every layer (attention-output SAEs 0.9-1.7x). Rescaling the true state to the reconstruction's norm costs almost nothing, so direction and not shrinkage is the cause; the whole KL distribution shifts; substituting at a single token still shows the gap over the following 16 tokens. Engels et al. (abstract and introduction only): about half of the SAE error vector and over 90 % of its norm can be predicted linearly from the state itself, and larger SAEs fail on the same tokens as smaller ones.
entries.relevance: The first half of U4 repeats the standard measurement, and its comparison with equal-size random noise is this result; with the fairer baseline of Lee and Heimersheim the excess largely disappears. For the denoising test it sets the bar: the SAE's own error is a structured perturbation at least as harmful as isotropic noise of equal size, so projection can only help if the injected noise is clearly larger than the SAE error. Measure |h - SAE(h)|/|h| first; with 81 % variance explained it is at most about 0.44 of the centred norm, the same order as f = 0.3. U2's 'SAE error' class is a predictable, state-dependent direction, not an irregular one.

entries.topic: 6 Error terms and replacement models
entries.citation: Marks, Rager, Michaud, Belinkov, Bau, Mueller (2024). Sparse Feature Circuits. arXiv 2403.19647; Ameisen et al. (2025). Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models. transformer-circuits.pub
entries.finding: Marks et al. write each state as SAE features plus an error term and keep the error term as a node of the circuit, so the model's computation is unchanged; their linear attribution underestimates effects in the layer-0 MLP and early residual layers. Ameisen et al. replace all MLPs by a cross-layer transcoder: the pure replacement model reproduces the model's top next token in about 50 % of cases for their best 18-layer dictionary (tested on tokens the model predicts correctly with under 80 % confidence; normalised reconstruction error about 11.5 %, 21.7 % for Claude 3.5 Haiku). Errors compound across layers, so per prompt they add error nodes and freeze attention and normalisation. Perturbation effects in that local replacement agree with the real model one layer on (cosine about 0.8) and diverge over further layers. On an out-of-distribution prompt almost all nodes were error nodes. Thresholded raw neurons serve as a baseline, with the remark that stronger neuron activations are more interpretable.
entries.relevance: Two established ways to run a dictionary alongside a model: keep the error term and write back only edits (the network is not disturbed), or replace outright (errors compound; half the predictions change even for the best published dictionary). An SAE that communicates in real time (H2) would use the first, and then the only disturbance is the edit itself. U4's full replacement at several blocks should be expected to compound. The neuron-threshold baseline is prior art for the claim that few strong activations suffice.

entries.topic: 6 SAE inserted in the forward pass as a filter
entries.citation: Saiyed, Sadiekh, Agarwal (2026). Towards Understanding the Robustness of Sparse Autoencoders. arXiv 2604.18756
entries.finding: Pretrained SAEs are inserted into the residual stream at inference (state replaced by its reconstruction, weights unchanged, gradients passed through) in Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, LLaMA-3 8B/70B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Median success of optimised jailbreak suffixes falls from 55.0 % to 19.05 % (GCG) and from 19.35 % to 9.7 % (BEAST) over six models; suffixes optimised on the plain model transfer poorly to the SAE model. Fewer active latents give more protection (monotonic). Early layers protect most but disturb normal behaviour, middle layers balance, late layers do little; in Qwen2.5 transfer success drops from 58.8 % to 32.4 % with the SAE at layer 19 and to 0 % at layer 7. I found no comparison with a non-sparse projection of equal reconstruction quality in the paper.
entries.relevance: The closest existing result to 'SAE as a filter in the forward pass', including a Qwen model: it removes adversarially optimised input structure, at a cost to clean behaviour that is largest in the low layers. It does not test random activation noise and lacks the PCA and neuron-basis controls planned in U4, which are therefore the new part. For H2 it indicates that the low layers are where an inserted SAE changes the network most. Related (abstract only): Li et al. 2023, arXiv 2210.06313, report that enforcing top-k sparsity of MLP activations improves robustness to input corruption and calibration.

entries.topic: 6 Closed loops between a controller or SAE and the model
entries.citation: Skifstad, Yang, Chou (2026). Local Linearity of LLMs Enables Activation Steering via Model-Based Linear Optimal Control. arXiv 2604.19018; related: Chen, Engels, Tegmark (2025). Low-Rank Adapting Models for Sparse Autoencoders. arXiv 2501.19406; Cho, Wu, Koshiyama (2026). Control Reinforcement Learning. arXiv 2602.10437
entries.finding: Skifstad et al. (read in part) treat the forward pass as a linear time-varying system over layers, compute feedback gains from per-layer Jacobians (linear quadratic regulator) and correct the state at every layer towards a set-point during generation. They show that Jacobians at a given layer are similar across reachable states and dominated by a few modes, and derive tracking-error bounds; eight models including Qwen-2.5 3B/14B/32B. No SAE is involved. Chen et al. (abstract and introduction only): fine-tuning the model with low-rank adapters around a frozen SAE cuts the loss gap of the inserted SAE by 30-55 %. Cho et al. (abstract only): a learned policy picks one SAE feature to amplify at each token in Gemma 2 2B. The Qwen-Scope report uses SAE feature activations as an auxiliary loss during fine-tuning and cuts unwanted language switching by more than half in most settings.
entries.relevance: Real-time closed loops between a controller and the network exist, with a linear theory of how a correction propagates through the layers; SAE-based loops exist at training time (adapters, auxiliary loss) and as per-token feature selection. None reports a mechanism inside the network that limits the loop's disturbance; stability comes from the controller design. Local linearity implies that in the small-f range the response in U2 should scale with f; departures from that are the plateau effect.

entries.topic: 7 Qwen-Scope SAEs
entries.citation: Deng, Wang, Wang, Wan, Ma, Yang et al. (2026). Qwen-Scope: Turning Sparse Features into Development Tools for Large Language Models. arXiv 2605.11887; model card Qwen/SAE-Res-Qwen3-1.7B-Base-W32K-L0_50
entries.finding: TopK SAEs on the residual stream after every block of seven Qwen3/3.5 models; for Qwen3-1.7B-Base width 32,768 with exactly 50 (or 100) active latents per position. Trained on activations 'sampled from in-house pretraining data', with an auxiliary loss (weight 1/32) against dead latents; activations with extremely large norm were filtered out (most frequent in Qwen3-1.7B and 8B, mainly the first token). The paper and the model card report no reconstruction quality at all (no variance explained, no loss after insertion). All SAEs except those for Qwen3.5-27B are trained on base models; transfer to chat models is not measured, the card only states that using them on post-training checkpoints 'is also reasonable'. The paper's table numbers layers 1-28, the card's files 0-27.
entries.relevance: U4 has to establish the basic quality of these SAEs on the chat model itself; there is no published number to compare with. A TopK SAE always returns 50 active latents, also for a noisy state, so it cannot abstain, which matters for the denoising test. Positions with extreme norm were excluded in training and must be excluded or handled in U2 and U4.

entries.topic: 7 Transfer of SAEs from base to chat models
entries.citation: Kissane, Krzyzanowski, Conmy, Nanda (2024). SAEs (usually) Transfer Between Base and Chat Models. LessWrong / Alignment Forum, 18 Jul 2024
entries.finding: SAEs trained on a middle residual layer of a base model reconstruct the chat model almost as well, and vice versa, for Mistral-7B and Qwen1.5-0.5B: inserted into Mistral-7B-Instruct the base SAE recovers 98.85 % of the loss against 99.01 % for the chat SAE (variance explained 60.9 % against 69.2 %, with more active latents). It fails for Gemma v1 2B, whose weights differ unusually between base and chat, and on the under 1 % of activations with outlier norm (BOS, early positions), which cause cascading errors when inserted. On chat-formatted text both SAEs are worse (variance explained 50-63 % instead of 61-69 %). Fine-tuning the base SAE on 5M chat tokens closes the gap.
entries.relevance: Makes it plausible that the Qwen-Scope base SAEs carry over to the Qwen3 chat model, but the evidence is for an older, smaller Qwen and one middle layer. It also accounts for the project's low 56 % at the last template token: SAEs trained on plain text are weaker on chat formatting. For U4, drop outlier-norm positions and report content and template tokens separately.

entries.topic: 7 SAEs trained on the Qwen3-1.7B chat model
entries.citation: He, Wang, Zhao, Ren, Li, Qiao, Wei, Qu (2026). Discovering Millions of Interpretable Features with Sparse Autoencoders (Qwen3-Instruct SAE). arXiv 2606.26620; model card adamkarvonen/qwen3-1.7b-saes
entries.finding: He et al.: JumpReLU SAEs trained on the instruction-tuned Qwen3-1.7B itself (also 4B, part of 8B) for every layer at three sites: residual stream, MLP output, attention output; widths 16K and 65K, L0 80 and 160, 5B tokens of FineWeb-Edu (plain text). Loss after insertion (figures only, no numbers in the text) is nearly recovered in the first two layers, clearly worse in layers 2-4 and improves again from layer 5 to 27; residual and MLP SAEs recover more than attention SAEs; L0 hardly changes variance explained but improves loss. The paper says the suite is released; I found no download link in its text. Karvonen's card for the SAEs the project uses: BatchTopK with a fixed threshold, trained on 90 % FineWeb and 10 % LMSYS-Chat, 500M tokens; activations above 10x the median norm were filtered because Qwen models have attention-sink tokens hundreds of tokens into a text (about 0.1 % of tokens, norms 100-1,000x the median); an eval_results.json sits next to each SAE.
entries.relevance: A known depth profile for the chat model: SAE insertion hurts most at layers 2-4, where U4's block 2 lies. If the weights can be obtained, chat-trained SAEs exist for all blocks and for MLP outputs. The outlier tokens matter for U2: with the relative size f defined per position, a perturbation at a sink token is 100-1,000x larger in absolute terms and can dominate through attention; exclude or cap those positions.

entries.topic: 8 Noise stability of trained networks and its link to generalisation
entries.citation: Arora, Ge, Neyshabur, Zhang (2018). Stronger generalization bounds for deep nets via a compression approach. arXiv 1802.05296; Morcos, Barrett, Rabinowitz, Botvinick (2018). On the importance of single directions for generalization. arXiv 1803.06959
entries.finding: Arora et al.: in VGG-19 on CIFAR-10, Gaussian noise with 10 % of the norm of a layer's input shrinks rapidly in relative size as it passes through higher layers. This 'noise stability' is formalised (a layer's signal is aligned with the few large singular directions of its weights, noise is spread over all) and shown to imply that layers can be compressed, which yields generalisation bounds; an AlexNet trained on shuffled labels differs in these measures in the direction of less stability. Morcos et al.: networks trained on partly corrupted labels are consistently more sensitive to Gaussian noise added to all hidden units, and to cumulative ablation of units, than networks trained on true labels; reliance on single directions predicts generalisation across 200 CIFAR-10 networks and over the course of training. Both read in the relevant sections via ar5iv.
entries.relevance: The triangle the user proposes, compressibility, damping of noise in hidden states, generalisation, is established for vision networks, as a property of all layers and not as a separate mechanism (weak form of H1). U2's decay of the relative deviation for isotropic noise and U6's expectation that damping grows as the network generalises both have this precedent. New would be the comparison by direction type and the per-block write-against measure in a transformer.

entries.topic: 8 Robustness and regular structure appearing during grokking
entries.citation: Humayun, Balestriero, Baraniuk (2024). Deep Networks Always Grok and Here is Why. arXiv 2402.15555; related, abstracts only: Nanda et al. (2023) arXiv 2301.05217; Merrill, Tsilivis, Shukla (2023) arXiv 2303.11873; Doshi, Das, He, Gromov (2023) arXiv 2310.13061
entries.finding: Humayun et al.: robustness to adversarial inputs appears long after test accuracy has converged ('delayed robustness') in MLPs, CNNs, ResNets and a small GPT. The density of linear regions around data points first rises, then falls as the regions move towards the decision boundary, so the function becomes smoother near the data; the same migration is shown for the MLP layers of a transformer grokking modular addition; batch normalisation removes the effect. From abstracts: Nanda et al. split grokking on modular addition into memorisation, gradual circuit formation and a late 'cleanup' that removes memorising components; Merrill et al. find a sparse subnetwork of few neurons with growing norm taking over at the transition; Doshi et al. show that with corrupted labels the memorising neurons can be identified and pruned, and that weight decay and dropout make all neurons generalising.
entries.relevance: For U6: smoothing of the function around the data at or after grokking is known for input perturbations, including one modular-arithmetic transformer; the residual-stream version by direction type is not. Robustness may lag generalisation, so checkpoints must extend well past the grok step into the cleanup phase. The memorising and generalising neuron populations give a U3-style per-neuron analysis a ground truth in this setting.

entries.topic: 8 Self-correcting trajectories in a trained LLM
entries.citation: Fernando, Guitchounts (2025). Transformer Dynamics: A neuroscientific approach to interpretability of large language models. arXiv 2502.12131; Lad, Lee, Gurnee, Tegmark (2024). The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference? arXiv 2406.19384
entries.finding: Fernando and Guitchounts (Llama 3.1 8B): residual states are replaced at a chosen layer by points on a grid in the plane of the first two principal components ('teleporting'). After replacement at layers 7, 15 and 23, trajectories return towards the unperturbed one with low variance; after replacement at layer 0 or 31 they end far away. The authors call this self-correcting, attractor-like dynamics and name noise injection as the missing, more realistic test. Lad et al. (abstract and parts): deleting or swapping adjacent layers leaves 72-95 % of top-1 predictions unchanged in GPT-2 and Pythia models; the first layer is the exception, its removal gives very high-entropy outputs; final layers sharpen the distribution with suppression neurons.
entries.relevance: Direct evidence that perturbations are corrected in the middle of the network and not at the bottom: the lowest block is the least forgiving place, contrary to the role H2 gives it. U2 is the experiment these authors call for, with finite perturbations of defined type. U5's baseline should note that disturbing block 0 already produces high entropy without any regulation.

entries.topic: 8 Theory: iterative refinement, contraction to the data manifold, error correction
entries.citation: Jastrzebski et al. (2018). Residual Connections Encourage Iterative Inference. arXiv 1710.04773; Greff, Srivastava, Schmidhuber (2017). Highway and Residual Networks learn Unrolled Iterative Estimation. arXiv 1612.07771; Alain, Bengio (2014). What Regularized Auto-Encoders Learn from the Data Generating Distribution. arXiv 1211.4246; Yu et al. (2023). White-Box Transformers via Sparse Rate Reduction. arXiv 2306.01129; Hanni, Mendel, Vaintrob, Chan (2024). Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition. arXiv 2408.05451
entries.finding: From the abstracts. Residual blocks refine one running estimate instead of computing new representations, later blocks moving features along the negative gradient of the loss (Greff; Jastrzebski). The reconstruction of a denoising or contractive autoencoder minus its input estimates the gradient of the log data density, so it points back to the data manifold (Alain and Bengio). A transformer block can be derived as one step of compressing token sets towards a mixture of low-dimensional subspaces (attention) followed by sparsification (MLP), and networks built that way work (Yu et al.). Networks that compute in superposition need explicit error-correction layers to keep interference noise from accumulating with depth (Hanni et al.).
entries.relevance: These are the candidate explanations U2 and U6 have to tell apart: damping as a by-product of every block refining an estimate, as contraction towards the data manifold, or as error correction required by superposition. All predict stronger correction of off-manifold (irregular) directions and none predicts a separate monitoring mechanism, so a positive U2 result alone does not establish H1's internal UFO. The compression-plus-sparsification reading is the nearest formal statement of H1.

entries.topic: H2 worst case: random activation noise and fine-tuned behaviour
entries.citation: Shahani, Miandoab, Scheutz (2025). Noise Injection Systemically Degrades Large Language Model Safety Guardrails. arXiv 2505.13500
entries.finding: Gaussian noise added to all activation layers at inference raises the rate of harmful outputs by up to 30 % (p < 0.001) in chat models of the Gemma, Llama-3, Yi and Qwen2 families, at noise levels that keep the text coherent. Deeper safety fine-tuning gives only marginal protection; training with noise protects only inside the trained range (sharp loss of protection between sigma 0.2 and 0.24 for Gemma 2B). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is the exception: it goes from refusing directly to incoherent output with only a narrow harmful stage, which the authors attribute to its reinforcement-learning post-training.
entries.relevance: Bears on H2's worst case: random activation noise is not absorbed harmlessly; behaviour added by fine-tuning breaks before general fluency does, so no general brake protects it. For the project (side effects of fine-tuning) this means U2's read-outs should include a fine-tuned behaviour and not only KL on plain text, and that Qwen models may differ from other families.

already_known: Overall: mostly a repeat of known results are the first half of U5, the first half of U4, the output-KL-by-direction part of U2, the compressibility half of U6 and the linear part of U1. Mostly new are U3, the denoising half of U4, the persistence measure in U2 and the damping half of U6.

U1 (linear part): that z-scored activations are far more compressible than a version with each neuron shuffled independently is expected and largely known. Activations of trained networks lie near low-dimensional manifolds (cited in the UFO paper: Ansuini 2019, Recanatesi 2019; for transformers and 28 LLMs: Valeriani 2023 and Joshi 2025, abstracts only; Sanyal 2020: effective rank about 10 at the last layer of a ResNet without any regulariser). The shuffle control removes all correlation between neurons, which a randomly initialised network also has, so it cannot show that training produced the structure. Not measured before: the 2-dim non-linear bottleneck on LLM neuron activations. A randomly initialised model as control and held-out examples would make U1 informative.

U2 (output KL by direction class at one layer): this is the design of Lee and Heimersheim 2024 and Heimersheim and Mendel 2024 on GPT-2 small. Known result: isotropic random directions change the output least, covariance-matched random directions and differences of two real states more, differences that include minus the current state most; SAE decoder directions beat isotropic random; the SAE-error direction behaves like covariance-matched noise. The dependence on size is the activation plateau (also in Qwen2, Janiak 2024): small deviations are suppressed and larger ones break through, so damping does not grow with f. Decay of the relative deviation with depth follows from the growth of the residual norm (Heimersheim and Turner 2023) and was shown for Gaussian noise in a vision network by Arora 2018. New in U2: the persistence p_m and which block writes against the perturbation.

U3: partly known for a narrower case. After ablation of attention heads, sparse and prompt-specific sets of late MLP neurons reduce their erasure, and about 30 % of the repair runs through the final normalisation scale (Rushing and Nanda 2024); late MLPs push down the top token (McGrath 2023). Whether the same holds for generic residual perturbations is not known, so U3 is not a repeat, but the share of the normalisation has to be taken out first.

U4, first half (loss and KL after replacing the state by its SAE reconstruction): standard SAE evaluation. For the chat model such numbers exist in the eval_results.json next to each of Karvonen's SAEs and as layer profiles in He et al. 2026 (worst at layers 2-4); the comparison with equal-size random noise is Gurnee 2024 (2.2-4.5x worse in GPT-2) as corrected by Lee and Heimersheim 2024. Only the Qwen-Scope base SAEs on the chat model have no published number. The second half (SAE as denoiser against PCA and the neuron basis) was not found anywhere.

U5, first half (finding entropy neurons by large write norm and small effect through the unembedding, clamp test): replicates Gurnee et al. 2024 and Stolfo et al. 2024 (GPT-2, Pythia, Phi-2, Gemma 2B, LLaMA2-7B) and Du et al. 2025 (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, base and instruct) in a model family where it has not been shown. The mechanism is known: writes into directions the unembedding ignores change the final normalisation scale and with it the entropy. The response to injected noise is new, but a rise of entropy with added norm is the expected mechanical effect.

U6, compressibility over checkpoints: repeats Kazanskii 2026 in linear form (effective dimensionality collapses before grokking in transformers and MLPs on modular addition and division) and, for UFO-regularised runs only, appendix D of the UFO paper; the gradual emergence of regular neuron maps is Nanda et al. 2023 and figure 6 of the UFO paper. The damping half has precedents for input noise (Humayun 2024, including a transformer on modular addition) and for hidden-unit noise in vision networks (Morcos 2018, Arora 2018), but not for residual perturbations of defined type across grokking.
gaps: Reconstruction quality of the Qwen-Scope SAEs (variance explained, loss after insertion): neither the paper nor the model card gives any figure. Measured transfer of these base-model SAEs to the Qwen3 chat model: none found; the only measured Qwen case is Qwen1.5-0.5B at one middle layer (Kissane 2024).
Entropy or confidence-regulation neurons in any Qwen model: nothing found.

An SAE or any other projection used to remove injected activation noise, with a PCA or neuron-basis control of equal reconstruction quality: nothing found. Nearest: SAE insertion against jailbreak suffixes (Saiyed 2026), without such a control.

A per-block account of which attention or MLP writes act against a generic residual perturbation (the persistence measure of U2 and U3): nothing found. Nearest: self-repair after ablations and Jacobian spectra.

A Lyapunov spectrum of a trained language model: not found; only Jacobian eigenvalue and singular-value analyses, and Lyapunov exponents for random initialisation (Cowsik et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.02579, abstract only).

A UFO-style measurement (2-dim non-linear bottleneck) on MLP neuron activations of a language model, or any test for a UFO-like internal mechanism in a conventionally trained network: nothing found. A self-modelling auxiliary task that makes networks simpler exists (Premakumar et al. 2024, arXiv 2407.10188, abstract only), but it has to be added and is not shown to arise by itself.
Robustness of hidden states to noise across grokking checkpoints on modular arithmetic, by direction type: nothing found.

A real-time loop in which an SAE reads the state, decides and writes back with feedback at every token: found only per-token feature selection by a learned policy (abstract only) and feedback controllers without SAEs.
Discussion, replication or critique of the UFO paper: none found; its arXiv listing is dated 9 Nov 2026.
Download location and numeric scores of the Qwen3-Instruct SAE suite (He et al. 2026): the paper shows figures only and its text contains no link.

Not read, by rule: the Goodfire essay and Atlas; for these I relied on the project README and a search-result summary of a podcast about the essay. Not fetched: Brown et al. 2022 (dimension drop before grokking, cited by the UFO paper), Gao et al. 2024, Templeton et al. 2024.

result.verdict: U2 to U5 can test H2 and a run-time reading of H1 (something in the forward pass that pushes states back towards the data subspace), but not the UFO of the paper, which acts only through gradients during training; that part rests on U1 and U6. As planned, the headline measures would report 'irregular directions are damped, regular ones amplified, damping depends on size' without any mechanism behind it: the residual norm grows about 100-fold with depth, the 'regular' direction removes the current state, and RMSNorm alone weakens responses at large f. The smoke run of ufo_damp.py (2 texts, indicative only) shows what actually has to be explained: the MLPs remove about 20 % of an injected vector per block, independent of its size, while the absolute deviation grows about 50-fold and the output KL at f = 0.3 is of the same order for all direction classes. The biggest weakness is reading the persistence p as damping: it tracks whether the injected vector is still in the stream, not whether its effect was contained. The run needs local and absolute estimators, covariance-matched noise inside the data subspace as the comparison class, and a write-level test of whether the erasure protects the output.

points.problem: The residual norm grows about 100-fold with depth, so the relative deviation |h'_m - h_m| / |h_m| falls without any damping. Running text (smoke run of ufo_damp.py, 2 texts): mean norm 16.9 / 28.0 / 69.1 / 178 / 987 / 2827 / 2525 after blocks 0 / 2 / 8 / 14 / 21 / 26 / 27. Last prompt token (256 stored prompts): 14.3 / 25.8 / 56.7 / 152 / 1067 / 2968 / 1640. A vector that no block touches (p = 1), injected at relative size f after block 2, has relative size 0.011 f at the output; from block 14 it is 0.07 f. In the smoke run the relative deviation for random directions injected at block 2 falls from 0.30 to 0.17 while the absolute deviation |h'_m - h_m| / |delta| rises to 50 (68 from block 0, 18 from block 8, 6.7 from block 14). What looks like damping is a 50-fold growth that is only slightly slower than the growth of the stream.
points.change: Do not use the relative deviation as evidence. Report amp_m = |h'_m - h_m| / |delta| with the split amp^2 = p^2 + s^2 (s = part orthogonal to delta), and the growth of the deviation relative to the growth of the stream, amp_m |h_l| / |h_m| (1 = neutral). Speak of damping only if amp_m < 1, or, in relative terms, only in comparison with covariance-matched noise inside the data subspace at equal norm. Report m = 26 and m = 27 separately, because the last block removes a large common component (see U5-3).

points.problem: The identity p_m = p_(m-1) - ka_m - km_m is exact (o_proj and down_proj are linear and bias-free; it holds to two decimals in the smoke data), so the arithmetic has no double counting. The reading has four problems. (1) p = 1 is the free value through the skip connection: it says that no block wrote along delta, not that the state is intact. (2) p < 1 says that the injected vector was overwritten, not that its effect was contained: one block after injection at block 2 the smoke run has p = 0.78 and amp = 1.07, so the block removes 0.22 delta and adds about 0.73 |delta| in other directions. (3) After three to four blocks the deviation is 5 to 50 times |delta| and nearly orthogonal to it; ka_m and km_m of later blocks are then projections of an unrelated propagated deviation onto delta (for 'reg' at block 2: km = -0.72 at block 16, ka = +0.82 at block 26), not responses to delta. Adding them up as each block's restoring contribution is double counting in the causal sense. (4) p does not predict the output: at f = 0.3 the classes end with p between 0.05 and 2 and with KL between 0.03 and 0.13 nats. For small f and a sign-symmetric class, the expected change of p in the next block equals trace(J P_S) / dim S, the mean eigenvalue of that block's Jacobian on the subspace S; p is a trace estimate.
points.change: (a) Local estimator, one extra pass per condition: after every block overwrite the perturbed stream with clean_m + f |h_m| u_m (a fresh unit vector of the same class) and record the write difference of the next block; q_m = -<write difference, delta> / |delta|^2, for attention and MLP separately, is the erasure coefficient of every block, free of propagation and of norm growth. Isotropic noise and the difference of two states of a second clean text in the same batch need no per-block basis. (b) Restoring index R_m = -cos(write difference, delta): chance level is about 1/sqrt(2048) = 0.02; the smoke numbers imply about 0.29 at block 3. (c) In the free-running runs read ka and km only up to three blocks after the injection, as a hazard (ka_m + km_m) / p_(m-1). (d) State-level measures are trace estimates over about 55 positions per text: 8 to 16 texts are enough; spend the texts on KL.

points.problem: 'reg' in the draft is unit(h_other - h): it contains minus the current state. Lee and Heimersheim (arXiv 2410.12555) showed that exactly this 'difference' direction is an unfair baseline (it 'includes the negative of the original activation') and changes the output more than a mixture of two other activations. On running text two random states are probably about as far apart as a state is long (the mean vector is 55 to 66 % of the norm in the smoke pool), so 'reg' at f = 1 replaces the state at every position >= 4 by roughly another token's state: KL 7.8 to 9.5 nats and the same top token at 0 to 7 % of positions. Its p of up to 13 is the divergence of two real trajectories under 100-fold norm growth (stored states: the difference between two prompts at block 2 projects with coefficient 8 on itself at block 21 while the cosine is 0.03), not amplification of a perturbation. Ordinary content shows the pattern without any perturbation: at the last prompt token each block's write regresses on the existing prompt-specific state with -0.07 to -0.32 in blocks 1 to 14 and +0.02 to +0.24 in blocks 15 to 25 (observational, 256 prompts). The class is also not sign-symmetric, so its p contains even-order terms. 'Irregular damped, regular amplified' is therefore guaranteed by construction.
points.change: Use two on-manifold classes that are sign-symmetric and do not contain the current state: 'mix' = h_a - h_b of two pool states, and 'covmix' = difference of two Gaussian draws with the pool covariance. Keep the move towards a real state only as a separately labelled content-swap reference, parametrised by the fraction alpha of the way (0.3 and 1; alpha = 1 is a real state). Draw each unit direction once and reuse it for all sizes.

points.problem: The 'lowest-variance principal subspace' is partly a sampling artefact. In the smoke run the pool has 1,204 states in 2,048 dimensions: at least 845 of the 1,170 to 1,346 'irregular' dimensions are exact null directions of the sample. The full pool (about 4,400 to 4,900 autocorrelated states) has full rank, but the cut 'last 1 % of in-sample variance' stays optimistic: on stored states (block 14, 1,472 prompts) the top 512 principal axes of one half hold 99.5 % of the in-sample but 94.0 % of the held-out variance, and 4.6 % of held-out variance lies outside the span of all 736 training states. The pool mean direction (55 to 66 % of the norm, no variance) can end up inside the 'irregular' subspace. Isotropic 'rand' is not a separate class: 57 to 66 % of its dimensions are the 'irregular' ones.
points.change: irr = random vector in the orthogonal complement of the top k principal axes, with the mean direction projected out. Choose k on held-out texts so that the complement holds at most 1 to 2 % of held-out variance, and print that share. Pool of at least 150 texts (about 9,000 states, 3 to 4 minutes). Keep isotropic noise at one size as the literature baseline only. The decisive pair is covmix (inside) against irr (outside): same norm, same generator, same sign symmetry.

points.problem: RMSNorm alone makes responses depend on f. A delta orthogonal to h of relative size f reaches every later block as sin(theta) = f / sqrt(1 + f^2) (0.0995 / 0.287 / 0.707 for f = 0.1 / 0.3 / 1.0), and the clean signal is scaled by cos(theta) (0.995 / 0.958 / 0.707). Per unit delta every linear response therefore weakens by cos(theta), and at f = 1 every later block also writes a different clean signal. The smoke run follows this null: p one block after injection is 0.78 / 0.78 / 0.80 (block 2), 0.79 / 0.80 / 0.88 (block 8), 0.90 / 0.91 / 0.95 (block 14) for f = 0.1 / 0.3 / 1.0. The erasure is independent of size (linear) and weakens at f = 1; nothing so far looks like a brake that engages for large perturbations. In addition f is measured against |h|, most of which is a constant mean vector; at a fixed token role natural states differ by only 0.10 to 0.12 |h| at blocks 0 to 2 (0.41 at block 14), and on running text f = 1 is about the distance to another token's state.
points.change: (1) Sizes f = 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0 for the two main classes (0.03 anchors the linear regime), reported also in natural units |delta| / median |h_a - h_b| at that block. (2) Plot responses against sin(theta) and test the brake as a deviation from linearity: log-log slope of the orthogonal deviation s (1 = linear) and of KL (2 = linear) between neighbouring sizes, bootstrap over texts. A slope above linear at small sizes is a plateau (small perturbations suppressed); a slope below linear at large sizes beyond the cos(theta) factor is a brake. (3) Two controls per block: norm only, h' = sqrt(1 + f^2) h (invisible to the next RMSNorm; isolates the changed weight of the old stream against later writes), and norm-preserving, h' = (h + delta) |h| / |h + delta|. (4) Print the radial share cos^2(delta, h) of every class.

points.problem: At equal norm, noise and real differences put their energy in different places, and tolerance to isotropic noise needs no mechanism. Last prompt token, block 14 (1,472 stored states): a real difference between two prompts has 88 % of its energy in the 220 dimensions that hold 90 % of held-out variance, an isotropic vector 10.8 % (= 220 / 2048). A random delta of size f |h| moves any fixed read-out direction by only about f in units of the rms of the state, while active features sit several such units out. That the same top token survives at 70 to 85 % of positions with noise as large as the state at every position (smoke, f = 1) follows from this.
points.change: Print for every class the share of its energy inside the top-k data subspace, and compare classes at equal norm and at equal energy inside that subspace. The noise that can test a mechanism is covariance-matched noise, which puts the same norm on the directions the network reads.

points.problem: The draft perturbs all positions >= 4 with independent directions. Attention then averages independent vectors (its share of the erasure is small in the smoke run: summed ka 0.08 to 0.21 against km 0.60 to 0.87 from block 2), and the deviation at a position mixes the local response with perturbations imported from earlier positions; with one vector at all positions the imports would add up coherently (the steering case). Which of the three is meant decides what 'local' means in H2. First positions and sink tokens: both SAE families were trained without states of extreme norm (Karvonen readme: about 0.1 % of tokens, 100 to 1000 times the median, not only at the first token; Qwen-Scope report: outliers 'especially in activations associated with the first token'). The draft already skips norm > 10 x median and positions < 4, which is right, but it uses the mean norm, and template tokens inside the window (im_end, im_start assistant, think tags) serve as donors and targets.
points.change: Keep independent-per-position as the main condition. Add on 16 texts: (a) one perturbed position t0 >= 8, reading p, amp and KL at t0 and at later positions separately; (b) the same vector at all positions. Draw conclusions about a mechanism inside the blocks (U3) from (a). Log per block how many positions the norm filter removed, exclude template tokens from the donors, report wiki and chat texts separately, report KL by position, and use medians for norms.

points.problem: (a) Every SAE direction in the draft comes from Qwen-Scope SAEs trained on the base model with pretraining text; applied to the chat model they explain 86 / 80 / 68 % of variance at blocks 0 / 2 / 8 (smoke pool), with a relative error of 0.25 / 0.33 / 0.45 |h|. Whether the decline with depth is the SAE or the drift from base to chat model cannot be told from these SAEs alone. (b) The SAE error is not an 'irregular' direction: only 40 / 35 / 25 % of its energy lies in the low-variance subspace that has 66 / 61 / 57 % of the dimensions; in the smoke run it is erased early like noise (p 0.78, 0.58, 0.49) and written back later like content (p about 1 at blocks 21 to 25). This fits the README (the unexplained rest separates the categories almost as well as the whole state). It also has a radial part, since these SAEs shrink the norm (roughly 15 % of the error energy for the block-21 SAE, from its published cosine 0.92 and norm ratio 0.925), and RMSNorm cannot see a radial change. (c) 'saedec' takes the strongest unit at another position; if a few dense units dominate, the class collapses to a few fixed directions, and 0.3 |h| along one decoder direction is far above a unit's natural activation.
points.change: Split one mixture direction D = h_a - h_b with the SAE into its decodable part SAE(h_a) - SAE(h_b) and its error part and inject both at the same norm next to D itself: same content, same positions, only the split differs. For single units follow Lee and Heimersheim: alive, not active in the sequence, active on fewer than 10 % of pool positions, size in units of the unit's own 95th-percentile activation; print how many distinct units were used. Calibrate the base-model SAEs against a chat-model SAE on the same tokens: block 21 will have both (Karvonen file is local, Qwen-Scope layer 21 is being downloaded); the Karvonen SAE for block 14 (resid_post_layer_14/trainer_0, 268 MB) gives a second point.

points.problem: Directions are drawn anew for every size, so size comparisons are unpaired. log-softmax runs in float32 and there is no numerical floor. Means over positions of ratios can be carried by single tokens (the spikes at blocks 16 and 26 come from two texts). The loss change is much noisier than KL (several negative loss changes in the smoke run).
points.change: Pair directions across sizes; add a second clean row as a null condition; log-softmax in float64 as in neu_sparsity.py; store per-position values, report medians and a bootstrap over texts; KL is the primary output measure, loss only with a paired interval. Fix the primary contrasts and thresholds before the run (see falsifiers).

points.problem: There is no architectural baseline: an erasure of about 0.2 per block or a restoring index of 0.3 could be a property of the trained weights or of the pre-norm SwiGLU architecture.
points.change: At the end of the run re-initialise the weights in place (same instance, no extra memory) and repeat the local-estimator pass on 8 texts (about 1 minute). In U6 the checkpoint at step 0 plays the same role.

points.problem: c_n as planned is divided by |delta|, so it does not add up to km, and its sign is opposite to ka and km in the draft. More important, the test is circular: choosing the N neurons with the most restoring c_n and clamping them raises p by construction (the direct part is exactly the sum of their c_n). With zero-mean contributions of spread sigma the 100 / 1,000 most negative of 6,144 add up to about -250 sigma / -1,510 sigma, while the net total has a standard deviation of 78 sigma: selection alone looks like a concentrated mechanism. For one random delta, c_n = (g_n . delta)(w_n . delta) / |delta|^2 has a signal-to-noise ratio of |cos(g_n, w_n)|, so a ranking from the perturbed run is mostly noise. Random neurons are mostly inactive (README 6.4: no effect at all) and control nothing. README 6.3 already found gross contributions 2.2 times the net.
points.change: c_n := -(a'_n - a_n) <w_n, delta> / |delta|^2, so that the c_n of a block add up to km. Select neurons on other texts and other delta draws than those of the test, or from the closed form in U3-2. Controls: the N most amplifying neurons (mirror image), N neurons matched in |a'_n - a_n| |w_n|, the whole MLP, the attention output. Report net, gross and both tails.

points.problem: In the linear regime the per-neuron attribution needs no perturbation runs at all, and the planned empirical version is noisy and biased by selection.

misreadings: The facts in the summary are right (2-dim bottleneck in grokking, z-scored activations, selective update, 2-12x and 114x); the items below are over-readings and omissions. First: the UFO is treated as something a network could contain and use at run time ('internal UFO-like mechanism', damping of perturbations). In the paper it is a second network that acts only through gradients during training and has no part in the forward pass: 'UFOs do not directly write or update weights, but instead partially influence the weights by learning to compress representations found in patterns of activations.' and 'The reconstruction errors from the UFO are used to update the primary parameters'. The paper-faithful tests are U1 and U6; U2 to U5 test a different idea.

H1 is presented as following from the paper. For conventional training the paper expects the opposite: 'The FER evident in the conventional gradient descent baseline representations shown in Figure 11 suggests that we should not expect UFR to emerge from conventional training.' and 'Until now, no general method has existed to encourage UFR.' What it reports without a UFO is regular structure emerging gradually in a grokking run with weight decay ('the highly regular response patterns of each component at the grok step are apparent in fuzzy and partial ways earlier in training'): regular representations, not an organiser.

'Names post-hoc SAEs and co-trained SAEs as relatives': the paper sets both apart from UFOs. Co-trained: 'The co-trained SAEs encourage the transformer's residual stream activations to be sparsely decomposable into features of an overcomplete SAE, rather than compressible by a low-dimensional bottleneck as in UFOs.' Post hoc: 'in contrast to UFO autoencoders that are co-trained with another network to encourage better representations in that network, SAEs are commonly trained post hoc to describe the internal activations of an already-trained network'. Nothing in the paper says that an SAE supports the UFO geometry; a post-hoc SAE exerts no pressure on the network at all.

'2-12x faster with weight decay' leaves out the control that matters for H1: a frozen, randomly initialised autoencoder already gives 2.39x (MLP) and 2.97x (attention) in the intercomponent case, against 3.16x and 7.54x for the selective UFO. Paper: 'the fixed treatment (wherein weights in g_phi do not update from their small initialization) achieves a lower median grok step than both the weight-decay-only control and the non-selective control in the intercomponent cases. One hypothesis is that even a randomly initialized UFO imposes a low-dimensional constraint that is useful in this setting.' For the intercomponent MLP UFO planned as the comparison in U6, most of the gain therefore needs no model of regularities.

'Up to 114x without' is the median of the best treatment, which grokked in 6 of 8 seeds; its MLP counterpart mostly failed: 'In particular, the intracomponent MLP case only leads to grokking for one of eight seeds'.

'Regular' is equated with UFR. The paper claims the aim, not the result: 'The autoencoder-based auxiliary loss function is intended to lead to UFR as seen in Picbreeder networks', and 'Although UFO-regularized results are not always consistent (the random seed used for network initialization can influence representational quality and poorly tuned hyperparameters can lead to underfitting)'.

Scope for U1 on running text: 'the implementations presented here rely on fixed-length sequences wherein there are consistent roles for each position in the sequence across inputs'. Only the fixed-token-role variant of U1 corresponds to the paper.

Not a misreading of the summary but a deviation in execution: the grokking job now running uses weight decay 0.3 (folder grok_base_s0_wd0.3). Paper: 'All experiments with weight decay use a weight decay of 0.03.'

result.verdict: Only in part. U1 and U6 can test the weak form of H1, that the activations of a normally trained network become compressible as it generalises; nothing in the plan tests an internal mechanism, because the paper's UFO is a second network that acts through gradients during training and is absent at inference, the paper itself does not expect conventional training to yield such representations, and it has not been checked that UFO training produces damping at all (a one-seed look at the two toy runs on disk shows no clear difference). H2's real-time, non-deterministic loop is not run anywhere: every experiment is a single open-loop forward pass with fixed vectors, so U2 to U5 can speak against a brake for large perturbations but cannot confirm H2. The biggest weakness is that no contrast separates 'developed for generalisation' from architecture, normalisation, weight decay and training time: U1 has only a shuffle floor, in-sample fits with fewer examples than neurons and a 2-dim bottleneck that in the paper equals the two free variables of the input domain, and U6 is one run at ten times the paper's weight decay with perturbation sizes tied to constant vectors and read-outs on problems the network answers wrongly before grokking. The toy runs on disk already bound H1 (one seed each): after grokking, two dimensions explain 12 % of the second MLP layer of the weight-decay-only network on held-out problems, against 98 to 100 % in the UFO-trained network, which gets there partly by emptying the regularised position.

points.problem: Damping of perturbations at inference is not what the paper's UFO does. The UFO is a second network that exists only during training and changes the first one through the gradient of its reconstruction error (paper: "UFOs do not directly write or update weights, but instead partially influence the weights by learning to compress representations found in patterns of activations."). The text contains no statement about perturbations, noise or behaviour at inference. A network trained with a UFO is therefore expected to have compressible activations; that it also pushes disturbed states back is an added assumption. Damping also has causes that need no organiser (growth of the stream norm, normalisation, a read-out that uses few directions, weight decay), and the predicted sign is open: a direction the network never reads passes through untouched (persistence 1, no effect on the output), which is the opposite of 'damped more than regular ones'.
points.change: State H1 as three separate claims, each with its own measurement. (a) Outcome: without any regulariser, activations become compressible by a small bottleneck as the network generalises (U1, U6). (b) Training dynamics: the ordinary update of a normal run lowers the UFO loss (H1-3; toy model only, not testable in the finished Qwen model). (c) Run-time mechanism: later blocks cancel components of the state that lie off the data manifold (U2, U3, H1-4). A positive U2 result supports (c) only, and only with the controls of the U2 to U5 review; it says nothing about (a) or (b).

points.problem: The damping detector has no positive control. Nobody has shown that a network trained with a UFO damps irregular perturbations more than a network trained with weight decay alone; until then neither a positive nor a null result in Qwen bears on H1. A first look at the two toy runs on disk (one seed each, weight decay 0.3; own read-only diagnostic) shows no separation. Isotropic noise of 0.3 times the state norm after block 0 at '=': both networks keep the answer on 97 to 100 % of the training problems once they generalise (ceiling). Noise as large as the state at all positions: the UFO run keeps 13 to 56 %, the baseline 8 to 33 %, depending on the checkpoint.
points.change: Calibrate on the toy pair before interpreting Qwen: at least 5 seeds per arm (17 to 25 minutes per run at the measured speed), compared at equal validation loss, not at equal step. If the UFO arm is not clearly more tolerant than the baseline, drop damping as evidence for H1.

points.change: In the weight-decay-only run co-train a selective UFO that only reads (lambda = 0, the paper's schedules) and log its loss on all examples in 200-step windows as in figure 19, with a non-selective twin. At every logged step compute g, the gradient of that loss with respect to the transformer's weights, and the first-order change of the loss caused by the step actually taken, separately for the Adam step on the task loss and for the weight-decay step (minus learning rate times weight decay times the weights): <g, task step> and <g, decay step>. The dynamic form of H1 predicts a negative <g, task step> on average before the grok step; if only the decay part is negative, compressibility is a by-product of weight decay. The bottleneck is 2 wide there (4 in one image run), so it matches the degrees of freedom of the input domain, and the autoencoder's limited hidden width measures how simple the map from those two variables to the activations is. Prompts from 18 question families, or running text, have no such structure: 2 dimensions can at best separate a few families (50 principal axes of the state give 86 % family accuracy, README section 1). The figure would describe the prompt set, and a low value would say nothing about regularity. The paper also names a fixed sequence format as a precondition ("the implementations presented here rely on fixed-length sequences wherein there are consistent roles for each position in the sequence across inputs.").
