Held-out share of the second MLP layer through the 2-dim autoencoder (trained for the probe's 300 steps): 24 % at random initialisation, 9 % while the network memorises (step 5,000), 13 to 14 % after it generalises (step 13,000). The probe's in-sample figures have the same order (31 / 20 / 22 to 26 %).
points.change: Same inputs, same split and same code for: (1) the randomly initialised Qwen (the switch RANDINIT=1 exists in ufo_damp.py; run it after the trained model, one model in memory at a time); (2) a Gaussian surrogate with the mean and covariance of the real activations: its linear curve matches by construction, so 'autoencoder minus 2 principal components' on real against surrogate data isolates curved structure; (3) the same block in a randomly rotated basis, z-scored after the rotation: z-scoring gives every neuron equal weight, so the measure is tied to the neuron basis, and this shows by how much; (4) shuffling within question family, which keeps the family means; (5) the input of block 0 at the same positions as input baseline. Report differences to (1) and (2), not raw levels.

points.problem: The paper z-scores every hidden node over a batch of 512 examples at one token role and reconstructs with a mean squared error, so every node counts the same whatever it writes. Three things differ in Qwen. (1) Activations are concentrated and heavy-tailed (25 % of the neurons carry 96 % of the squared activation per block, README 6.1); z-scoring turns the few events of a rarely active neuron into values of many standard deviations that dominate the error and do not recur on held-out examples. (2) Neurons that are constant at the token role become all-zero columns under the paper's rule (division by the larger of the standard deviation and 1e-6) and count as perfectly reconstructed; dropping them, as the toy probe does, changes the number of columns between blocks and checkpoints (toy first layer: 452 varying nodes at step 1,000, 150 at step 13,000). At step 15,000 the error left after 8 dimensions is 22 % over the varying nodes and 7 % counted the paper's way. (3) A share of z-scored variance does not say what the reconstruction is worth to the model.
points.change: Per block report the number of varying neurons, the share of squared z-values beyond 5 standard deviations, and the measure in three versions: z-score over varying neurons, rank-normalised (or clipped at 5), and counted the paper's way. Add a functional read-out: write the de-normalised reconstruction back into the MLP of that block and give the loss increase in nats, next to +0.02 nats for keeping the strongest 50 % of activations (README 6.1).

points.problem: The planned autoencoder is trained on all examples. In the paper that is the non-selective control, the weakest of the three intercomponent variants for MLP activations (1.66x, against 3.16x for the selective UFO and 2.39x for a UFO that is never trained). The paper's UFO is updated only on the best-reconstructed tenth of the examples of each layer (starting from a quarter), sees a layer code and is shared by all layers, while the loss the network receives is computed on all examples.
points.change: Per block report the selective version next to the plain one: autoencoder trained with the paper's schedule on the best-reconstructed tenth, error given for all examples and for the selected tenth, plus the distribution of per-example errors and the question families the selected tenth comes from. That also tests the paper's conjecture for language models ("It is possible that well-covered topics more closely approach UFR while sparsely covered topics tend towards FER."). Train one autoencoder per block and say so; one 2-dim code shared across 28 blocks, as the paper shares it across 2, is not sensible.

points.problem: U1 covers one of the paper's four UFO types. Attention weights gave the larger speed-ups (12.25x and 7.54x, against 2.04x and 3.16x for MLP activations), and the intracomponent view, one neuron's responses over the whole input domain, is the one that connects to neurons as units. For a linear bottleneck the two views give the same number (the same singular values of the examples x neurons matrix, up to the bias term); they differ only for the non-linear autoencoder.
points.change: On the grid of U1-2: (1) intracomponent: each neuron's response map over the grid as one example for an autoencoder with a 2-dim bottleneck and 128-wide hidden layers, plus two direct regularity scores per neuron: the share of variance explained by additive effects of a and b and by the sum alone, and the concentration of the map's 2-D Fourier spectrum; (2) attention: the weights of the '=' query row over the 6 positions, all 16 heads of a block concatenated (96 numbers), autoencoder with an 8-wide hidden layer as in the paper.

points.problem: On running text the rows of the matrix are tokens with different identities and positions, a case the paper's setting excludes. In the lower blocks most of the z-scored variance is then token identity, and tokens of one text are not independent examples.
points.change: For running text either keep one role (for example the first token after a sentence end, or one frequent token) or remove each neuron's mean per token identity before z-scoring. Report per block the share of variance explained by token identity alone as a baseline, and split by text.

points.problem: The request assumes that an SAE supports the UFO geometry. The paper describes the two geometries as different: co-trained SAEs make activations sparsely decomposable "rather than compressible by a low-dimensional bottleneck as in UFOs". A state that is exactly a sparse sum of dictionary directions need not be compressible at all. With 12 of 8,192 units active in 512 dimensions (the ratios of the Qwen-Scope SAEs) the held-out share through 2 / 8 / 32 / 128 dimensions is 0.5 / 1.9 / 7.4 / 28 % when all units are equally frequent, the level of isotropic noise (0.4 / 1.6 / 6.2 / 25 %), and 5.6 / 16 / 34 / 58 % with Zipf-distributed frequencies (own synthetic check). Low-dimensional compressibility of SAE-decodable states thus reflects how unequal the unit frequencies are.
points.change: At the blocks that have an SAE apply the U1 measure to three matrices over the same tokens: the state, its SAE reconstruction and the SAE error, with the held-out split of U1-1. 'The SAE supports the UFO geometry' predicts that the reconstruction is clearly more compressible than the error. As frequency-only baseline add states decoded from the real SAE codes after shuffling each unit's activations independently across tokens.

points.problem: U6 is announced as the paper's own setting, but the run on disk is not. Weight decay is 0.3 instead of 0.03 (grok step 12,000 instead of the paper's median 98,000 within a budget of 150,000); all linear layers and the output layer have biases; the task loss is summed over the two target positions; training stops 8,000 steps after the grok step. With learning rate 1e-3 the decay time constant is 3,300 steps instead of 33,000, so the UFO schedules (warm-up until step 500, selectivity lowered over 2,000 steps) cover ten times more of the run. The paper leaves several choices unstated; it says the code is public and "builds on the original grokking code from Power" et al., but I could not open the repository in this session.
points.change: Copy from section 5.1 and Appendix C: 2-layer decoder-only transformer, width 128, 4 heads, MLP with 512 ReLU nodes, layer norm after each attention and each MLP block, learned token embeddings, fixed sinusoidal positions; tokens 0 to 96, '/', '=', <|eos|>; sequences <|eos|> x / y = z <|eos|>; cross-entropy on z and on the closing <|eos|>; a problem is correct only if both are right; 9,312 problems, a fixed half (4,656) for training, the same split in all runs; batches of 512, per epoch nine full batches and one of 48; AdamW, betas (0.90, 0.98), epsilon 1e-8, learning rate 1e-3 after 10 linear warm-up steps, weight decay 0.03 towards zero on all learnable parameters; validation accuracy every 1,000 steps, grok step = first recorded step with at least 99 %; 150,000 steps; eight seeds that set transformer initialisation, UFO initialisation and batch order. Intercomponent MLP UFO: the 512 MLP activations of one layer at '=', each node z-scored over the batch (divide by the larger of the standard deviation and 1e-6), with a 2-dim one-hot layer code at the encoder only; one autoencoder for both layers, one 128-wide hidden layer each in encoder and decoder, bottleneck 2; Adam, learning rate 1e-3 without warm-up, betas (0.90, 0.999), no weight decay; lambda 0 until step 250, linear to 1 at step 500; selectivity from 25 % to 10 % over the first 2,000 steps, per layer the examples with the lowest reconstruction error; first the transformer update (UFO frozen, gradients pass through it), then the UFO update with a stop-gradient on the activations; the partial batch is used (it is skipped only for intracomponent UFOs). Not stated in the paper, to be taken from its code: biases; dropout; initialisation and the scale of the token embeddings relative to the positional vectors (norm 8); tied or untied output layer; how the loss is averaged over the two target positions (this sets the weight of lambda against the task loss); whether activations are taken after the ReLU; the autoencoder's activation function, biases, bottleneck activation and 'small initialization'; whether the batch mean and standard deviation of the z-score carry gradients; how constant nodes enter the loss; the learning-rate schedule after the warm-up; the vocabulary size; the seed of the data split; numeric precision. Either run weight decay 0.03 once (150,000 steps are about 2 hours at the measured 20 steps per second) or label the series 'paper architecture, weight decay 0.3' and make no comparison with the paper's speed-ups.

points.problem: One run cannot separate generalisation from weight decay and training time, and the total weight norm is not a usable covariate. In the run on disk the total norm is 50.9 both at step 5,000 (validation accuracy 1.5 %) and at step 13,000 (100 %), but its parts moved in opposite directions: token-embedding matrix 28.6 against 8.4, attention of block 1 23.0 against 39.5, mean gain of three of the four layer norms 0.23 to 0.26 against 0.03 to 0.06. Sensitivity to directions the data do not use also depends on the optimiser alone: in a linear read-out trained with AdamW on inputs confined to a subspace, the gain on the unused directions after 12,000 steps was 0.08 to 0.68 of its starting value with weight decay 0.3 and 0.74 to 2.0 with 0.03, with nothing to generalise (own synthetic check).
points.change: (1) A control that cannot generalise, with the same optimiser, weight decay, steps and checkpoints: the same problems with the answers permuted once at random (the baseline memorises the true answers at 100 % up to step 7,500 with at most 3 % validation accuracy, so capacity under this weight decay suffices). (2) At least 3 seeds and 3 training fractions (for example 0.4, 0.5, 0.7) so that grok steps differ. Plot every measure against step, against the norms of the single matrices and against validation loss. Attribution to generalisation requires that the curves of different runs coincide on validation loss and not on step or norm, and that the label-permuted run stays flat. (3) Log per-matrix norms and layer-norm gains at every checkpoint. (4) Prefer contrasts inside one checkpoint (training against held-out problems, U6-3), which hold weights and time fixed.

points.problem: The probe fits the bottleneck on the training problems and scores it on the same problems, and it reads the perturbation effects on held-out problems only. Before grokking the network answers those wrongly (1.5 % correct), so 'still correct' rests on about 70 chance hits and the other read-outs measure the stability of wrong answers. On the training problems, answered correctly from step 1,000 on, the same isotropic perturbation (0.3 times the state norm after block 0 at '=') leaves the answer unchanged in 81 / 47 / 64 / 72 % of problems at steps 1,000 / 5,000 / 7,500 / 10,000 and in 97 / 100 / 100 % at steps 12,000 / 13,000 / 20,000; on held-out problems the series is 33 / 16 / 22 / 25 % and 87 / 98 / 100 % (own diagnostic). The rise at the grok step is real but about half as large as the held-out read-out suggests, and tolerance fell from 81 to 47 % while the network was still memorising.
points.change: Primary series on the training problems; held-out problems as second series. For compressibility add the transfer figure: z-score statistics, principal directions and autoencoder fitted on training problems, share of variance explained on held-out problems. A code shared by seen and unseen problems is the signature specific to generalisation, and it is a contrast inside one checkpoint. First values (own check on the saved checkpoints, 8 principal dimensions, fitted / held-out): first MLP layer 38 / 30 % at step 0, 25 / 10 % at step 5,000 (memorising), 57 / 57 % at step 13,000, 67 / 64 % at step 20,000; second layer 26 / 26 % at step 5,000 and 42 / 42 % at step 13,000, so there the linear structure is shared even while the network memorises.

points.problem: The relative size f is measured against the whole state, most of which is constant across problems, and the constant share changes during training. At the embedding the state is the token embedding plus a fixed positional vector of norm 8.0, and weight decay shrinks the token part from 8.5 (step 1,000) to 2.8 (5,000), 0.86 (12,000) and 0.66 (20,000): f = 0.3 is 0.4 times the token-specific signal at step 1,000 and 3.6 times at step 20,000. The probe's result at this site (answer changed in 94 to 95 % of problems after grokking) is this artefact. Scaled to the token part, f = 0.3 changes no answer after grokking, and at f = 1 the share of unchanged training answers rises 13 / 21 / 28 / 39 / 69 / 82 / 94 % over steps 1,000 / 5,000 / 7,500 / 10,000 / 12,000 / 13,000 / 20,000. After block 0 the state at '=' is 90 to 97 % (by norm) one constant vector.
points.change: Define size in units of the spread between real states at the site (median distance of two real states, or the norm of the state minus the site mean) and report the absolute size too. Where a site carries no information the test is void: in the UFO run the state after block 0 at '=' is identical for all problems at steps 15,000 and 17,000. Perturb the operand positions or all positions as well.

points.problem: The direction classes change meaning between checkpoints, and the post-norm architecture produces size-dependent damping by itself. The subspace holding 99 % of the variance after block 0 shrinks from 72 of 128 dimensions (step 1,000) to 29 (grok step) and 11 (step 20,000). 'Irregular' (the remaining 1 %) therefore grows from 56 to 117 dimensions and after grokking equals isotropic noise (KL 0.03 for both at step 20,000); a larger tolerance to it is the same fact as the drop in dimensionality, not a second finding. In a post-norm network a sublayer that ignores the injected vector completely still returns persistence 1/sqrt(1 + r^2 + f^2), with r the ratio of write norm to stream norm (measured 0.8 to 1.0 from step 1,000 on): 0.70 at f = 0.1 and 0.57 at f = 1 for r = 1. The probe has no measure of writes against the injected vector at all, so 'active' damping cannot be concluded from it.
points.change: Replace the 1 % cut by classes of fixed dimension (random vector in the top 8 and in the bottom 64 principal directions of the real states, mean and all-ones direction removed) plus covariance-matched noise, and print the dimension that holds 99 % of the variance. The state has 128 dimensions, so compute the exact Jacobian of the answer logits with respect to the state at each site and report its gain along the principal directions ordered by variance. Use finite perturbations for the dose series only and judge them against the layer-norm-only value.

points.problem: The toy compressibility figures need four corrections. (1) The probe's 2-dim autoencoder (300 full-batch steps, one seed, scored on the problems it was fitted on) is neither converged nor valid out of sample. Second layer at step 13,000: 23 % on the fitted problems after 300 steps and 30 % after 1,500, but 13 to 14 % and 5 % on held-out problems (two seeds agree), where 2 principal components give 12 %. Out of sample the non-linear bottleneck adds nothing to two linear dimensions in this layer, and longer training makes it worse. (2) Around the grok step two thirds of the first-layer nodes stop varying at '=' (U1-4), so 'more compressible' partly means 'fewer nodes left'. (3) A 2-dim bottleneck with 128 hidden units can in principle reproduce any function of a variable with about a hundred values, however irregular. Once the last MLP layer depends on the answer z alone, a high value certifies no regular code; such collapse onto the class is described for the training examples of classifiers trained far beyond zero training error (neural collapse, Papyan, Han and Donoho, arXiv 2008.08186) and by itself says nothing about held-out inputs. (4) The level at initialisation is not zero (U1-3).
points.change: Use the complete 97 x 96 grid, which allows an exact variance decomposition per hidden node: share explained by x alone, by y alone, by both main effects together, and by z alone, for training and held-out cells separately; plus the concentration of each node's 2-D Fourier spectrum, the regularity the paper shows in its figure 6. Report medians per layer and checkpoint next to the bottleneck figures and the number of varying nodes, all as differences to step 0 and to the label-permuted control. Autoencoder as in U1-1.

points.problem: The optional UFO run can be read neither as a replication nor as a picture of UFO-organised activations without checks. One seed per arm at weight decay 0.3 gave grok steps 9,000 against 12,000 (1.33x; paper: 3.16x as a ratio of medians over eight seeds at 0.03). And the regulariser was satisfied by emptying the regularised position: at steps 15,000 and 17,000 none of the 512 first-layer nodes varies across problems at '=' (their columns are zero after z-scoring and count as perfectly reconstructed; logged auxiliary loss 0.0001 at step 16,000), and from step 10,000 the second layer is 98 to 100 % explained by 2 linear dimensions with 87 to 97 % of its entries positive, that is, nearly linear. The paper's argument that the network "cannot trivially minimize" the loss "by shrinking its activation magnitude" does not cover constant nodes, and only the '=' position is regularised, so the computation can move to the operand positions. Validation accuracy also fell back to 99.5 % at step 17,000.
points.change: For every UFO run report the number of varying nodes per layer and the auxiliary loss with constant nodes excluded, and check where the operands are combined (attention pattern of block 1 at '=', variance of the states at the operand positions). For any statement about speed use at least 5 seeds per arm with the fixed-UFO and non-selective controls of the paper's table 1, or make none. Use the UFO arm mainly as the positive control of H1-2.

points.problem: 'Before' and 'after' grokking are not two states. In the run on disk validation accuracy goes 3.8 / 7.9 / 27.5 / 88.6 / 100 % at steps 8,000 to 12,000, and only the checkpoints 7,500, 10,000 and 12,000 fall into that stretch; training accuracy drops to 89 % at steps 8,000 and 9,000 (a loss spike); and the measures keep moving until the run ends 8,000 steps after the grok step (subspace with 99 % of the variance after block 0: 29 dimensions at step 12,000, 11 at step 20,000; varying first-layer nodes: 150 at step 13,000, 240 at step 20,000). The paper, Nanda et al. and Kazanskii describe a gradual emergence before the jump in accuracy, so the hypothesis has to be stated as an order of events in time.
points.change: Save every 500 steps from the first rise of validation loss until it has settled, continue for at least five decay time constants after the grok step (about 17,000 steps at weight decay 0.3), and use validation loss as the time axis. State beforehand which order H1 predicts (compressibility and tolerance reach half of their final change before validation accuracy does) and test it across seeds.

points.problem: H2 speaks of communication in real time that may be non-deterministic. All planned runs are single forward passes over given text with one fixed vector per position: nothing is fed back, nothing varies between repetitions and no text is generated. Such runs can show that a brake for large perturbations is absent; they cannot show that a loop is stable.
points.change: One closed-loop run: free generation of 32 tokens for 16 prompts with the key-value cache, at every generated token a fresh perturbation after block l (or the SAE read-modify-write step with the error term kept), 3 noise seeds. Read-outs as a function of the number of generated tokens: KL to the clean model's next-token distribution on the same prefix, and the divergence of the generated text from the clean continuation. A stabilising mechanism predicts a level per-token KL; accumulation shows as growth with length and as spread across seeds.

misreadings: Sentence 1, 'small': for the intracomponent variant the UFO is not small. Its input and output have one entry per problem (9,312) or per pixel (65,536), which by my count gives about 2.4 million weights against about 0.4 million in the transformer; only the bottleneck is small. Paper: "This additional computational overhead is most pronounced in the intracomponent case because the large input and output dimensionality significantly increases the UFO parameter count compared to the intercomponent case."

Sentence 1, 'normalised activations': the z-score is always taken per hidden node over the examples of the batch, also for the intercomponent variant; an intercomponent vector is one row of that column-normalised matrix and is not normalised within the layer. Paper: "intracomponent and intercomponent regularization are two different ways of regularizing the same hidden node activation matrix"

Sentence 1, omission: in the grokking experiments only the '=' position is read and regularised (for attention only the '=' query row), and one UFO serves both layers with a layer code that only the encoder sees. Paper: "is processing the = token to predict the next token z in an equation x / y = z." and "For both attention cases, only attention edges from a =-query row are regularized"

Sentence 2, 'regular' equals unified factored representations: this is the authors' working hypothesis and intention, not a result. No measure of UFR is reported for the transformer, and the implication is stated from regular to compressible only. Paper: "this paper builds on the hypothesis that such regularity is essential to good representation." and "Because regular representations are more likely to be compressible in this way"

Sentence 2, omission: the auxiliary loss is switched on gradually (zero until step 250, full from step 500 in the grokking runs) and is a soft constraint that the network can trade against the task; in the image experiment it cost fit. Paper: "Strong UFO regularization early in training risks preventing the primary network" and "both UFO-regularized networks slightly underfit the small butterfly body compared to the unregularized network"

Sentence 3, 'selective': correct, with two omissions. The fraction is lowered to 10 % (from 25 % over 2,000 steps for intercomponent, from 50 % over 33,333 steps for intracomponent UFOs). And selection is not what carries the intercomponent effect: a UFO that is never trained gives 2.39x (MLP) and 2.97x (attention), more than the trained non-selective one (1.66x, 2.39x). Paper: "achieves a lower median grok step than both the weight-decay-only control and the non-selective control in the intercomponent cases." and "One hypothesis is that even a randomly initialized UFO imposes a low-dimensional constraint that is useful in this setting."

Sentence 4, Picbreeder: the result is qualitative and shown for selected successful runs; no number measures regularity. Paper: "Although UFO-regularized results are not always consistent (the random seed used for network initialization can influence representational quality and poorly tuned hyperparameters can lead to underfitting)"

Sentence 4, '2-12x': the range pools two kinds of UFO. For MLP activations, which U1 and U6 use, the speed-ups are 2.04x (intracomponent, 7 of 8 seeds grokked) and 3.16x (intercomponent); 12.25x and 7.54x are for attention weights. Paper: "regularizing attention can lead to greater grokking acceleration than regularizing MLP activations (though MLP setups still perform multiple times better than weight decay alone)"

Sentence 4, 'up to 114x without': this is the intracomponent attention UFO, with 6 of 8 seeds grokking. Without weight decay the intracomponent MLP UFO fails and the intercomponent MLP UFO gives 19.02x. All speed-ups are ratios of median grok steps over eight seeds, read every 1,000 steps, in transformer steps (not compute), with hand-tuned settings and no intervals. Paper: "the intracomponent MLP case only leads to grokking for one of eight seeds" and "The UFO regularization hyperparameters and autoencoder architectures for each treatment were determined through empirical trial and error testing."

Sentence 5, SAEs as relatives: post-hoc SAEs are named as the contrast (they describe, they do not shape), co-trained SAEs as related with three stated differences (site, geometry, purpose). The paper does not say that an SAE supports the UFO geometry; it sets the two geometries apart. Its nearest relatives are co-trained low-capacity reconstructors. Paper: "rather than compressible by a low-dimensional bottleneck as in UFOs", "SAEs are commonly trained post hoc to describe the internal activations of an already-trained network" and "their method most closely resembles the intercomponent MLP UFOs introduced here."

Omission that bears on H1: the paper argues against the premise that normal training yields this organisation by itself. It grants only partial regularity that a UFO can amplify. Paper: "suggests that we should not expect UFR to emerge from conventional training." and "That conventional gradient descent leads to some representational regularity is promising because the UFO may be able to identify and amplify these regularities."

Omission that bears on H1 and H2: nothing in the paper concerns inference. The UFO is absent at run time and acts on the weights through training; the words perturbation, noise, damping and deterministic do not occur in the text, and robustness is mentioned once, for other authors' regularisers ("have shown promising results in improving network robustness"). Paper: "UFOs do not directly write or update weights, but instead partially influence the weights by learning to compress representations found in patterns of activations."

Omission that bears on running text and on Qwen: the method presupposes a fixed sequence format, the paper covers small models only, and for language models it offers conjecture and expects a mixed picture by topic. Paper: "the implementations presented here rely on fixed-length sequences wherein there are consistent roles for each position in the sequence across inputs.", "Although in this paper UFOs are only applied to small models in small domains" and "It is possible that well-covered topics more closely approach UFR while sparsely covered topics tend towards FER."

Omission: the only compressibility curve in the paper (Appendix D) is for UFO-regularised runs; no UFO loss is shown for a normally trained network, so 'compressibility rises as a normal network generalises' is not a result of this paper (it cites others for a drop in dimensionality). Paper: "Each panel shows one selective UFO treatment with weight decay, using the seed with the median grok step, until the transformer groks."

Link to the starting point: the reference list contains neither the neuron essay nor the Atlas. The Goodfire items are an essay by Cammarata ('Neural networks are already clean', not read here, by rule), cited as a concession, and work on concept manifolds; the paper also does not equate hard-to-interpret units with fractured representations. Paper: "as recently suggested by Cammarata (2026), mechanistic interpretability today focuses to a large extent on describing, rather than evaluating, representations." and "That is not to say that uninterpretable representations are bad representations"
falsifiers: Against H1 (outcome, toy model): in weight-decay-only runs the held-out share of variance through a small bottleneck (2 and 8 linear dimensions, 2-dim autoencoder; MLP activations at '=') and the transfer of the fitted code from training to held-out problems do not rise before or at the grok step in most seeds, or they rise just as much in the label-permuted run that cannot generalise.

Against H1 (attribution): across seeds and training fractions the curves of compressibility and of noise tolerance coincide when plotted against step or against the norms of single weight matrices, and not when plotted against validation loss.

Against H1 (strength; already seen in one seed at weight decay 0.3): after grokking the weight-decay-only network stays far from the geometry a UFO enforces. Second MLP layer, held-out problems: 12 % through 2 linear dimensions and 13 to 14 % through the 2-dim autoencoder (22 to 24 % at initialisation), against 98 to 100 % through 2 dimensions in the UFO-trained run. If more seeds and weight decay 0.03 confirm this, a built-in organiser of comparable effect is excluded for this network; what remains is a weaker linear trend (8 dimensions: 26 % while memorising, 42 % after grokking).

Against H1 (training dynamics): with a read-only selective UFO attached to a normal run, the first-order change of its loss caused by the task-gradient step is not negative on average before the grok step, or only the weight-decay step lowers it.

Against damping as a sign of H1: UFO-trained toy networks (5 seeds) are no more tolerant of off-manifold perturbations than weight-decay-only networks at equal validation loss. Then no damping result in Qwen bears on H1, whatever U2 and U3 show.

Against H1 in Qwen (outcome): on held-out prompts the trained model's neuron activations are no more compressible than those of the randomly initialised model on the same inputs; the 2-dim autoencoder gains no more over 2 principal components than on a Gaussian surrogate with the same covariance; and on the two-operand grid the neurons' response maps are no more concentrated (additive or Fourier share) than at random initialisation.

Against H1 in Qwen (mechanism): the randomly initialised model shows the same erasure profile by direction class; or off-manifold vectors are simply passed along (persistence near 1, no write against them, no effect on the output); or on clean passes the later blocks write no more against the part of the state that a bottleneck or the SAE fails to reconstruct than against the reconstructed part.

Against the universal wording of H1 ('every normally trained network'): one clean counter-example suffices, for instance a toy run that reaches 99 % validation accuracy while the outcome, attribution and dynamics tests above come out null.

Against H2 (lowest layers): at equal size in units of the natural spread between states, perturbations after blocks 0 to 2 change the output at least as much as after blocks 8 and 14, and replacing the state by its SAE reconstruction costs most at block 2 (the project's literature step reports this profile for chat-model SAEs: worst at layers 2 to 4, He et al., arXiv 2606.26620).

Against H2 (a brake for large perturbations): after removing what normalisation alone does (norm-only and norm-preserving controls) the erasure per unit of injected vector does not increase with its size, and the output effect grows at least in proportion (KL at least quadratic in size, or a plateau followed by a jump). The smoke run of the U2 to U5 review already points this way: about 20 % erasure per block at every size.

Against H2 (a developed safety mechanism): the randomly initialised model gives the same erasure per block; or removing from the block writes their component along the injected vector leaves the output KL unchanged, so the erasure protects nothing.

Against H2 (SAE in the loop): at equal clean reconstruction quality the SAE projection passes on as much injected noise as a PCA projection, and with the SAE in the loop the output is further from the clean one than without it for noise up to the size of the SAE's own error.

Against H2 (confidence regulation): the entropy rise under early noise equals that of a late perturbation matched to the final deviation, and clamping the candidate neurons of block 27 does not change it.

Against H2 (real time): in free-running generation with a fresh perturbation at every generated token, the per-token KL to the clean model and the spread across noise seeds grow with the number of generated tokens instead of levelling off. Without such a run the real-time part of H2 is untested either way.
